title: The Destruction of Community
author: Michael Perrone
summary: Michael Perrone uses the history of college football as a case study in how institutions born from genuine community end up destroying it. A lifelong Texas Longhorns fan, he explains that the more he has experienced real community, the less enthusiasm he has for proxies of it. He then narrates five eras: students spontaneously creating teams and rivalries, universities institutionalizing that energy, scaling that converts relationships into roles, atomization in which bonds are replaced by contracts and brand loyalty, and finally dependence, where isolated individuals rely on the institution for meaning their communities once supplied. A court ruling reinstating a quarterback suspended for betting on his own games illustrates how contract law now outweighs the integrity of the group. His move is to generalize the pattern to families, churches, schools, and neighborhoods, warning that the youngest generations will navigate these hollowed institutions alone. Filed under Leadership as a close call because the argument concerns how organizations scale relationships into roles and is addressed to 'men who lead.'
points: Perrone's five-era model (creation, harvest, scale, atomization, dependence) describes how institutions consume the high-trust relationships that created them.
The key mechanism is scale: because relationships scale poorly, growing institutions convert people into roles such as student athlete, booster, and employee.
In the atomization stage, relational coherence is maintained only through contracts, illustrated by a court prioritizing a suspended quarterback's earning potential over team integrity.
The end state leaves individuals dependent on a single relationship with the institution for identity and meaning, with little relational infrastructure left elsewhere.
He argues the same roles-for-relationships pattern now runs through family life, churches, schools, and neighborhoods, with young people bearing the greatest cost.
quotes: Put simply, the more I’ve experienced of genuine community, and how it sustains people and builds power, the less enthusiasm I have for proxies.
And college football is an amazingly entertaining proxy of a genuine community; a perfect microcosm of the industrialization of human belonging.

Every institution began as a group of people who had high demand, high trust relationships and needed a name for what they were doing all day. Institutions use these bonds as a power source to preserve and enlarge the community.

The institution seeks to scale its capacity, resources, capital and prestige, all while trying to hold true to the original human connections that created it. But relationships and community scale poorly.
What happens when you scale something whose most essential component is relationship? Relationships become roles.
With the founding community now gone, only autonomous and interchangeable individuals remain. Any relational coherence now requires contracts.

At last, our journey is complete. We began with an institution that was built to preserve a fraternity of men. And we end with an institution that has only preserved itself by destroying the fraternity and isolating its members.

We live in a world of proxies. In family life, neighborhoods, schools, church, career, youth sports, government… everything. The same transformation of relationships into roles has permeated every connection.
